name: Core stability (plank, dead bug)

lead: Core stability training uses holds like the plank and controlled movements like the dead bug to train the trunk. Posture communities include it in pelvic tilt routines.
Encyclopedic sources say research support for the core stability model is limited, and nothing found tests it for appearance.

paras: The exercises train the abdominal, back and hip muscles to hold the spine and pelvis in position under load or movement.
Generally low risk. Back pain during exercise is usually referred to a clinician.

lead: Core stability is defined as a person's ability to control the tone, position and movement of the core, meaning the head, neck and torso. [1] The plank, an isometric hold resembling a push-up position, and the dead bug, a lying limb-movement drill, are common training exercises for it. [1][2]

In looksmaxxing and posture communities, core stability work is recommended as part of correcting anterior pelvic tilt and improving trunk posture. [3] Wikipedia lists planks, side planks and dead bugs among exercises suggested for that purpose, while flagging weak sourcing. [3]

Wikipedia states that there is little research support for the core stability model and that core-specific training performs about as well as general exercise at best, and cites a critical review titled "The myth of core stability". [1] Whether core training changes pelvic tilt or appearance has not been tested in studies found.

paras: The core muscles listed in encyclopedic sources include the pelvic floor, transversus abdominis, multifidus, internal and external obliques, rectus abdominis, erector spinae and diaphragm. Breathing can influence core posture and movement. [1]

The plank is also called a front hold or abdominal bridge. A forearm plank rests the body on the forearms and toes; variants include the side plank, reverse plank and extended plank. Primary muscles for the front plank are given as the erector spinae, rectus abdominis and transversus abdominis, with the shoulder girdle, glutes and legs as secondary. The side plank emphasises the obliques, transversus abdominis and hip abductors. [2]

Planks, side planks and dead bugs appear in posture programs alongside glute bridges and hip thrusts as anterior pelvic tilt measures. [3] Proponents link a stronger trunk with better posture and a leaner-looking midsection.

Wikipedia reports that trunk- or core-specific exercise has not been shown to prevent sports injuries or improve sports performance, and that the belief that core stability is essential for posture, lifting and preventing back pain is presented without citations. [1]

A review of 270 trials published in the British Journal of Sports Medicine, cited by Wikipedia, found isometric exercises including planks and wall sits were more effective than other exercise types for lowering blood pressure. [2] That finding concerns blood pressure, not posture or appearance.

No studies found testing plank or dead bug training for pelvic tilt or appearance. Studies of core stability training more broadly are summarised as showing limited advantage over general exercise. [1]
